resources.string: NexTools is free. No ads, no account.
Open-source components: AndroidX, Jetpack Compose, Kotlin (Apache 2.0).
Measurements are stored only on your phone. The internet is used only to check for updates.
The altimeter measures height difference from pressure difference. Choose the starting point:
Enter the altitude of where you are (map, sign, building info).
Reference %1$s · set %2$s hours ago. It drifts when the weather changes.
Set a reference for accurate altitude: call this 0, enter a known altitude or use GPS.
Add this point as a corner
Add points automatically while walking (every 3 m)
Wait a few seconds at each corner; accuracy is ±3–10 m. Not a substitute for a cadastral survey.
GNSS corner points; spherical area formula
Sea-level pressure is calculated from this altitude. You can look it up on a map or building info.
Very sensitive to change · absolute ±1–3 hPa
When on, one reading is taken about every 30 minutes (last 48 hours kept). Battery impact is negligible.
Enter your altitude to see sea-level pressure (Calibrate).
A simple rule, not a weather forecast.
Not enough data yet. Turn on the log; the trend appears after a few hours.
Current may be unreliable on some brands
The battery is hot (above 45 °C). Reduce charging and heavy use.
Distance is estimated from signal strength; walls, bodies and orientation can change it several-fold. Many phones change their address often for privacy.
Only the count and strongest signal are recorded
Bluetooth is off. Turn it on to scan.
Permission is needed to scan for nearby Bluetooth devices. Device addresses are not stored.
This tool uses the back camera. Images are processed on the phone only and never stored.
The colour in the target circle is measured. For more consistent results, first show a white sheet in the same light and press \"Show white card\".
No white balance · depends on light
Enter east declination as positive, west as negative.
The magnetic field differs from what is expected: metal, a magnet or electronics may be nearby.
Compass calibration is weak. Move the phone through the air in a figure 8 a few times.
The declination for true north is unknown. Allow location or enter it by hand (Calibrate).
Cover the lens completely and start
The phone is warm; sensor noise can cause false counts. Move it somewhere cool.
Light is leaking: cover the lens fully with black tape or put it somewhere dark.

Cover the lens with black electrical tape, lay the phone screen-up on a table and plug it in. At sea level very few hits per minute reach the sensor; meaningful results take hours. Some counts may come from natural radioactivity or sensor noise.
There is a crash log on this phone. You can share it for support; it is never sent automatically.
Raw data, note and photo will be deleted permanently.
%1$d / %2$d tools work on this phone · %3$d ready now
No gyroscope; lateral acceleration and turns can\'t be measured.
Longitudinal from GPS speed, lateral from speed × gyroscope yaw rate
The phone can sit in any orientation but must not move during the drive. The driver shouldn\'t handle the phone; let a passenger start it.
The value must be between %1$s and %2$s.
No favourites yet. Long-press a tool or tap the star on a tool screen to add one.
Stored only in this record, never sent anywhere.
High flicker — not recommended for long use
Moderate flicker — may tire sensitive people
The camera doesn\'t report its rolling-shutter skew; only the flicker percent is measured, frequency can\'t be shown.
Point the camera at a flat white surface (paper, wall) lit by the source; don\'t aim straight at the lamp.
Floor-to-floor height of one storey. Usually 2.8–3.2 m in homes.
Works in lifts and on stairs. Re-zero after a while because air pressure changes.
Display frozen. If recording, data is still being written.
Could not get GPS altitude. Try again outdoors or enter it by hand.
GPS altitude can be off by ±10–30 m.
Faded bars are satellites not used in the fix. The green line is 30 dB-Hz: above it is a good signal.
Dual-frequency (L1 + L5) receiver: more accurate positions.
Filled: used in fix · hollow: visible only. Centre is overhead, edge is the horizon.
The phone\'s location (GPS) service is off.
This tool needs precise location permission. Location is only shown on screen and never stored unless you record it.
The chip is unlocked with these three items printed on the card (also in the machine-readable zone on the back).
The country root (CSCA) chain is not checked; the result means \"chip data unaltered\", not official proof of validity.
Data group %1$d hash DOES NOT match
The chip refused access. Check the document number and dates.
Lost contact with the card. Try again without moving it.
This card is not an ICAO-compliant ID / passport chip.
Hold the card against the back of the phone
Keep the card still; reading can take 5–15 seconds.
Security object (SOD) could not be read
The photo couldn\'t be shown on this device (%1$s).
Data is only shown on this screen: not saved, not sent, screenshots are blocked. It is cleared when you leave the tool.
The chip\'s position varies; the phone\'s NFC antenna is usually in the middle or top of the back. A case can block reading.
Could not open the install confirmation.
The update is incompatible with this installation (the signature may differ).
Not enough free storage on the device.
Place the phone on a surface you know is level (or against a known vertical surface in edge mode) and set zero. Surface and edge modes are zeroed separately.
Lay the phone on a surface or stand it on its edge; the mode changes by itself. A case affects the reading: zero it with the case on for best results.
Cannot calibrate with this value. Try again somewhere brighter.
Hold the phone and a known lux meter at the same spot, facing the same way. The phone reads %1$s lx now. Enter the meter\'s value.
The sensor is usually next to the front camera. Hold the phone parallel to the surface you measure, without casting a shadow.
In brackets: baseline. The line on the bar marks the baseline.
Enter a machine name, put the phone on it and measure
This version uses the accelerometer only; a sound signature (microphone) will come in a later version.
Place the phone in the same spot and orientation each time and measure in the same operating state (e.g. spin cycle). This is not a diagnosis; it only tells whether something changed.
Earth\'s field zeroed at start; the value is the magnet\'s field at the sensor
The sensor saturated: the real value is higher than shown. Move the magnet a little farther.

Press Zero with the magnet away, then slowly bring it to the top of the phone (where the magnetometer usually is). The field falls fast with distance; compare magnets only at the same distance. Strong neodymium magnets saturate the sensor.
The field is very strong: a magnet or large metal object is nearby.
Tap the image to focus. Freeze it to read comfortably.
Not enough samples; hold the phone still for 2 seconds and try again.
The field moved too much; hold the phone steady and try again.
The ambient field is unusual (%1$d µT). Start at an empty spot away from large metal or magnets.
The anomaly is the difference from the ambient field at the start. Copper, aluminium, plastic pipes and unpowered cables cannot be found.
This tool is not definitive. Never use it as a safety tool before drilling or electrical work.
Hold the phone still, away from walls and metal objects, and start the scan. Then slide it slowly along the wall without rotating it.
Tempo is per smallest pulse (quarter or eighth). The large dot is the downbeat, the medium dot a group start. Usul groupings vary by tradition; enter your own under Custom if needed.
This tool needs microphone permission. No audio is recorded; it is processed on the phone only.
Tick the sensors you want below, pick a rate and press Record ●. All go into one CSV on a common timeline.
Common timeline %1$d Hz (each sensor\'s latest value is held)
The tag has no NDEF content or it could not be read.
Hold a tag against the back of the phone
Hold a tag near to write
Use the ID Card Reader tool for chip ID cards and e-passports.
Write failed; hold the tag still and try again.
The content is too large for this tag.
This tag does not support NDEF.
Existing content on the tag is replaced. Locked (read-only) tags cannot be written.
The notebook is empty. Press ● Record in a tool and measurements will collect here.
This tool cannot work without the required hardware. It turns on by itself on a phone that has it.
On this phone a camera-based fallback will be used; that mode arrives in a later version.
This report is built from what Android reports. Capabilities marked \"unknown\" can only be determined during a measurement.
This document records a measurement made with a phone. Values depend on the phone\'s sensors and calibration; use a calibrated instrument for official, legal or safety decisions.
NexTools %1$s · A measurement record; not a substitute for a certified, calibrated instrument.
Permission denied. You can also turn it on in Settings > Permissions.
Optional: true north, GPS altitude, location in records.
For the Sound Meter. No audio is recorded.
Not written yet; it will be added later.
This phone has the required hardware.
Stand still on the point and start
Estimated uncertainty of the mean position (1σ)
The receiver is using L1 only; dual-frequency (L1+L5) phones give clearly better results.

Put the phone still under open sky and wait at least 10–15 minutes. GNSS errors drift in the same direction for minutes, so a few minutes of averaging is not much better than a single fix. Without correction data the result is metre-level.
Angle between the red vertex and the two arms
Hold the camera square to the surface; an oblique view distorts the angle. Freezing the image makes dragging the points easier.
Not a medical device. Don\'t use it for health decisions.
Rest a fingertip lightly on the back camera and flash
Don\'t press hard; it blocks blood flow. The flash can get warm; keep measurements under 1–2 minutes.
This link is unencrypted (http). Check the address before opening.
Scanning uses Google Play services\' secure scanner; the app never sees the camera image.
The content is too long for a QR code.
Put the phone on a flat table and don\'t touch it. Each sensor is sampled for 3 seconds.
%1$d tools can be used right now in this version.
Values go to the map and the record only while moving (above 7 km/h).
Phone in a fixed car mount; depends on vehicle, tyres and speed
Put the phone in a fixed mount; in hand or on a seat the result is meaningless. Only runs with the same car at similar speeds are comparable.
Balanced — fine for a living room or office
Green: reliable · Orange: low range · Grey: not measurable
Very dead — good for speech, dry for music
The phone speaker plays bass weakly; 125–250 Hz values are unreliable.
External speaker + phone microphone, average of 3 sweeps
For bass bands use an external (wired, not Bluetooth) speaker.
Mid frequencies (500 Hz–1 kHz) could not be measured; the room may be too noisy or the volume too low.
Phone speaker + microphone, average of 3 sweeps
Dynamic range is low in some bands; values are approximate (T10/EDT instead of T20).
Slightly live — rugs, curtains, shelves help
Hold the phone in the middle of the room, away from surfaces. Stay quiet during the measurement. Bluetooth speakers cannot be used because of their latency.
Media volume is low. Turning it up and measuring again improves the result.
No RTT (802.11mc) access point nearby. Many home routers don\'t support it; some Google Wifi / Nest and enterprise access points do.
Wi-Fi RTT (time of flight), median of 10
Wi-Fi RTT needs Android 9 or later.
Pick an access point to range only it, more often. Walls and reflections lengthen the distance; line of sight gives the best result.
Wi-Fi RTT is unavailable right now. Wi-Fi and location must be on.
Enter the known length of the reference object in millimetres.
Drag the orange points to the ends of the reference and the blue points to the ends of the object.
The reference and the object must be in the same plane (e.g. on the same table) and the camera square to it. Lens distortion grows near the edges; keep things in the middle.
The screen turns black, white, red, green, blue and grey in turn. Look for dots of a different colour or ghost images; tap for the next colour.
Tap for the next colour · back to exit
Slide your finger across the whole screen; unresponsive squares stay grey. Multi-touch count is shown too. Press back to exit.
Close the door quickly; the pressure spike appears here

Close the windows, put the phone on a table inside the room, step out and close the door quickly. Tight room: big spike, slow decay. Leaky room: small spike, fast decay. Only tests with the same door and similar force are comparable; this is not a standard blower-door test.
The barometer is slow (%1$s Hz); short spikes may be missed and decay time is coarse.
A phone is not a sensitive seismometer; it gives no earthquake warning or magnitude.
High sensitivity counts small shakes too (footsteps, a door closing).
On Android 12+, rates above 200 Hz need a special permission; the app requests it.
Waiting for data… (some sensors only report when the value changes)
Calibrations are stored for this phone only. Resetting one returns the tool to its default values.
The app follows the phone\'s language. You can choose a different language for NexTools only.
The app follows the phone\'s language (Turkish or English).
The recording stays in memory only and is erased when you leave. Different sources may pick different microphones.
Almost no sound came from the microphone. The mic hole may be blocked or the microphone faulty.
On single-speaker phones left and right come from the same place. With headphones plugged in, sound goes to them.
Place the phone and a known sound meter in front of the same sound (a steady sound is best). The phone reads %1$s dB now. Enter the meter\'s value.
Use the same weighting (e.g. A) and time weighting.
The microphone is saturated: the sound is louder than the phone can measure. The real value is higher.
Could not open the microphone (code %1$d). Another app may be using it.
The Sound Meter needs microphone permission. No audio is recorded; only the level is calculated on your phone.
No audio is recorded. While recording, only levels are written to the Notebook.
The two points are too close; pick two different peaks.
Point at a compact fluorescent lamp. The blue (436 nm) and green (546 nm) lines are distinct; pick both and match their wavelengths.
The spectrum is faint; raise exposure or move closer to the light.
Not calibrated; x axis in pixels
The image is saturated; lower exposure (−1 / −2 EV).

1. Cut a ~2×2 cm piece of a CD or DVD (peel the DVD's top layer for a sharper spectrum).
2. Make a cardboard box or tube; cut a 0.5 mm slit at one end with a razor blade.
3. Put the disc piece at the other end at about 45°, with the camera behind it.
4. Aim the slit at the light; align the colour band horizontally on the dashed line.
5. Calibrate with a fluorescent lamp; don't move the setup after calibrating.
Time flows right to left; the vertical axis is log frequency (bottom: 30 Hz).
The phone doesn\'t provide raw GNSS measurements; clock and AGC checks are unavailable.
GNSS time differs from phone time

No indicator is proof on its own: indoors signals can be similar in strength, the phone\'s clock may be wrong. Several indicators at once raise suspicion. Real GPS jamming is common near airports and borders.
Lay the phone flat on the spinning surface
The phone isn\'t flat or is wobbling; the value may read low.
Gyroscope z axis; phone flat on the spinning surface
Near the gyroscope limit; the real speed may be higher.
Suits slowly spinning surfaces such as a turntable or a lazy Susan. Tape the phone down; it needn\'t be at the centre. The gyroscope limit is usually 300–1,000 rpm.
The measurement lab in your pocket
THE MEASUREMENT LAB IN YOUR POCKET
Be careful with headphones and high volume: high-frequency tones can harm hearing.
Compares the pressure jump when a door closes

When a door is closed quickly, the air in the room is compressed and pressure rises by a few pascals. The barometer measures this spike and its decay time: a tight room shows a big spike and slow decay, a leaky room a small and fast one.\n\nIt is a relative comparison between rooms, not a standard blower-door test. On phones with a slow barometer short spikes may be missed.
A relative comparison, not a standard blower-door test.

Calculates altitude change from pressure change (≈0.12 hPa ≈ 1 m). Excellent for relative height in lifts or on walks.\n\nAir pressure can change by a few hPa during the day, which means tens of metres of drift. Refresh the reference (here = 0 m, a known altitude, or GPS) now and then.
It drifts as the weather changes; refresh the reference from time to time.
Area by walking or on a map

Calculates area and perimeter by adding points at the corners of a plot or automatically while walking its edge: m², dönüm, hectares.\n\nArea uses a spherical polygon formula; the main error source is GPS accuracy. Not a substitute for a cadastral survey.
Not a substitute for a land survey.

Measures air pressure. If you enter your altitude, the sea-level pressure (the value in weather reports) is calculated.\n\nWith the optional pressure log, the app takes one reading about every 30 minutes and keeps the last 48 hours; the 3-hour change gives a simple weather trend.
The absolute value can be off by a few hPa; short-term changes are measured very well.

Shows battery percentage, temperature, voltage and instantaneous current, and calculates the charge or drain rate.\n\nThe unit and sign of the current vary by manufacturer; some phones don\'t report it at all.
Current readings are unreliable on some brands.
Lists nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices (watches, earbuds, beacons, phones) with signal strength and manufacturer. Distance is roughly estimated from signal strength.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.

Reads the average colour of a small area in the centre of the back camera: HEX, RGB, CIE Lab and the nearest colour name. The difference between two colours is calculated with CIEDE2000 (ΔE).\n\nThe camera\'s automatic white balance and the colour of the light affect the result; balancing with a white card is recommended. Not a substitute for a professional colorimeter.
Depends on the light; a white card for balance is recommended.

Finds the direction the phone points using the magnetometer and motion sensors. With location permission the declination comes from the World Magnetic Model (WMM) and true north is shown; otherwise you can enter it by hand.\n\nIf the field strength is far from the expected value, metal or a magnet is nearby and the reading is unreliable.
It goes wrong near metal and magnets; the app warns when it notices.
Counts bright tracks on a covered camera

With the lens fully covered and a long exposure, counts bright spots left by charged particles (muons etc.) hitting the sensor. Hot pixels that glow constantly are learned in the first frames and masked.\n\nExperimental: the sensor is small, so very few hits arrive per minute and a meaningful count takes hours. Heat and natural radioactivity can cause false counts; it is not a dosimeter.
Takes hours; heat causes false counts.
The phone\'s hardware, shareable as PDF

Shows which hardware the phone has and therefore which tools will work. Sensor vendors, maximum rates and resolutions are listed. \"Measure noise\" measures sensor noise while the phone rests on a table.\n\nShareable as PDF; handy when buying a used phone.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
Hard braking, harsh acceleration, cornering g

Detects harsh braking and acceleration from GPS speed changes and sharp turns from speed × gyroscope yaw rate; shows the current acceleration on a g-g diagram. The score is based on harsh events per kilometre.\n\nGPS speed updates once a second, so short sudden events are smoothed. Not an insurance or official driving assessment.
The phone must be mounted firmly in the vehicle.

The camera\'s line-by-line sensor (rolling shutter) takes a frame with a very short exposure. If the light flickers, horizontal bands appear; their depth gives the flicker percent and their spacing the frequency.\n\nResults vary with the camera and the surface; this is not an IEEE 1789 measurement. Very high-frequency flicker (above a few kHz) may not be visible.
Depends on the camera frame rate and scan direction.
Floors gained in lifts and stairs

Measures the height change from the start point with the barometer and divides it by the floor height to show how many floors you went up or down.\n\nVery reliable over short periods; it drifts as air pressure changes, so re-zero from time to time.

Watches for signs of GPS spoofing or interference: a mock location app, unusually equal or strong satellite signals, position jumps that speed can\'t explain, a gap between GNSS time and phone time, receiver clock discontinuities and automatic gain (AGC) drops.\n\nIt shows indicators, not a verdict. Clock and AGC checks need the phone to provide raw GNSS measurements.
Shows indicators, never a definite verdict.

Shows the satellites the phone sees (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, QZSS, NavIC), each one\'s signal strength and position in the sky. If the receiver also sees the L5/E5a band it is marked as dual-frequency.\n\nPosition accuracy is the ~68% confidence radius reported by Android.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.

Reads the identity data and photo from the chip of an ID card or e-passport (ICAO 9303). The chip is unlocked with the document number, date of birth and expiry printed on the card (PACE or BAC). Data group hashes and the document signer\'s signature are checked.\n\nData never leaves the phone and is not saved; screenshots are blocked. Since the country root certificate is not checked, it is not an official identity verification.
Needs the access data printed on the card; data never leaves the phone and is not stored.
Most new phones have no IR emitter.

Measures the direction of gravity with the accelerometer (or the gravity sensor). Lying on a surface it shows a two-axis bubble; standing on its edge it shows a single angle. The mode switches by itself.

Slope % = tan(angle) × 100. The zero point is stored for this phone only.

Does not measure flatness (bumps/dips), only the tilt where the phone touches.
A case or the phone\'s edge can add ±0.5° error; fix it with \"Set zero\".

Measures illuminance in lux with the ambient light sensor. The sensor is usually next to the front camera; hold the phone facing the light without casting a shadow.\n\nThe sensor is made for screen brightness; calibrate it against a known lux meter for accurate results.
Uncalibrated readings can be off by ±20%.
Compares a machine\'s vibration signature over time

The phone is placed on a running machine (washing machine, pump, fan…); a spectral signature is taken from 10 seconds of vibration and compared with the baseline saved for that machine: same, slight change or changed.\n\nIt doesn\'t diagnose; it only tells whether the vibration pattern or level has changed. Phone sampling is usually 200–500 Hz, so high-frequency bearing noise is not visible.
Not a diagnosis; it only says \"changed / not changed\".
Records the peak as you bring a magnet closer

Measures a magnet\'s field at the sensor using the phone\'s magnetometer. Earth\'s field is zeroed at the start; the increase and the peak are shown as the magnet comes closer.\n\nThe field falls very fast with distance, so the value is the field at that distance, not the magnet\'s \'strength\'. Phone sensors usually saturate at a few mT.
Measures only until the sensor saturates.
Three axes and total in µT

Measures the magnetic field on three axes and in total, in microtesla (µT). The Earth\'s field is about 25–65 µT depending on where you are.\n\nAndroid corrects for the phone\'s own magnetism in the background, so the value may jump slightly now and then.
Only low-frequency fields; it does not fully measure the 50/60 Hz mains field.
Uses the back camera at maximum zoom as a magnifier. The light (flash) can be turned on, tap to focus, freeze the image.\n\nNo image is stored.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.

The ambient field at an empty spot is taken as the baseline; while scanning, the deviation from it is measured. Iron and steel (nails, studs, rebar, iron pipes) disturb the field and are found. Live cables may leave a weak trace.\n\nCopper, aluminium, plastic pipes and unpowered cables cannot be found. This tool is not definitive and must never be used as a safety tool before electrical work.
Not definitive and never a safety tool before electrical work. Copper, plastic pipes and unpowered cables cannot be found.

An accented metronome with adjustable tempo: simple meters and asymmetric Turkish usuls (Türk Aksağı 5/8, Devr-i Hindî and Devr-i Turan 7/8, Aksak 9/8, Aksak Semâî 10/8) or your own grouping. Includes tap tempo and an optional vibration on the downbeat.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
Reads an NFC tag\'s ID, technology, capacity and NDEF content (text, links). Text or a link can be written to the tag, e.g. an asset tag.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
Reads pH paper or water turbidity colour
Compares against the paper\'s colour scale.
Averaged point fix with error ellipse

Takes a weighted average (by accuracy) of GPS fixes while you stay on one point; shows the scatter of individual fixes as a 95% ellipse and the estimated uncertainty of the mean.\n\nGNSS errors drift in the same direction for minutes, so the uncertainty assumes one independent sample per 60 s. Without correction data (RTK/PPP) the result is metre-level; not a substitute for a survey.
Angle between two lines in the camera view
Measures the angle between two arms and a vertex dragged on the camera image; the image can be frozen.\n\nIf the camera isn\'t square to the surface, perspective distorts the angle.

With a fingertip over the camera and flash, the amount of blood in the finger changes slightly with each heartbeat and the image brightness fluctuates (photoplethysmography). Beats per minute come from the frequency of this wave.\n\nNot a medical device; it doesn\'t measure arrhythmia, oxygen level or blood pressure. Movement and pressing distort the result.
Not a medical device; for curiosity only.

Scan: QR codes and barcodes are read with Google Play services\' secure scanner; the app needs no camera permission. For Wi-Fi codes, network name and password are shown.\n\nCreate: A QR code for text, a link or Wi-Fi details is generated entirely on the phone and can be shared as PNG.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
Colours road roughness on a map

Measures the vertical acceleration of a phone in a fixed car mount in 1-second windows and draws it on a colour-coded map with GPS position. Sudden large jolts are counted as potholes.\n\nThe value depends on the car, tyres, suspension and speed; it is not an absolute road index (IRI). Runs with the same car are comparable.
The phone must be mounted firmly in the vehicle.

Plays a rising sweep three times through the phone speaker, records it with the microphone and derives the room\'s impulse response. Reverb time (RT60: the time for sound to decay by 60 dB) is computed for each octave band; a larger value means a livelier room.\n\nThe phone speaker plays bass weakly, so the 125–250 Hz bands are often unreliable. The microphone is uncalibrated; this is not an ISO 3382 measurement.
Approximate; good enough to compare rooms.
Measure with AR or a reference object

Calculates the length of an object from a known-size reference in the same plane (bank card, A4 sheet or your own length) by proportion.\n\nThe reference and the object must be in the same plane and the camera square to it; otherwise the result is off.
Helps you find dead or stuck pixels and burn-in (OLED) with solid colours. The touch grid shows unresponsive areas and the multi-touch count. Handy when buying a used phone.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
Continuously records vibration on a table

Continuously plots the vibration of a phone resting on a table. When the short-term to long-term average ratio (STA/LTA) crosses the threshold, an event is marked — a simple method also used at seismic stations.\n\nIt gives no magnitude and is not a warning system.
Does not give earthquake magnitude; a phone is not a sensitive seismometer.
Live values and rates of all sensors
Lists every sensor in the phone. Tap a sensor to see its live raw values and the sample rate it actually reaches.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.
A rough measurement, ±10 cm or worse.

Filters the microphone signal with IEC 61672 A, C or Z weighting and calculates the Fast (125 ms) or Slow (1 s) time-weighted level, the equivalent continuous level (Leq) and the maximum (Lmax).\n\nNo audio is recorded; only levels are calculated on the phone. The microphone can saturate on very loud sounds; the app warns when it notices.
Uncalibrated readings can be off by ±5 dB or more.
Channel test, record and play back

Tests the speaker with left / right channels and a frequency sweep, and the microphone with a short record-and-play; shows the recording\'s peak and average level. Also lists the microphones the phone reports.\n\nThe recording stays in memory only and is not saved.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.

A diffraction grating (piece of CD/DVD) in front of the camera splits light into colours; the tool plots brightness along the dashed line. With a two-line calibration on a fluorescent lamp (436 and 546 nm) the x axis becomes nanometres. You can hold one light as a reference and compare others to it.\n\nThe camera\'s colour filters and automatic processing shape the spectrum; it doesn\'t measure absolute intensity and isn\'t a lab spectrometer.
Needs a simple home-made setup; a step-by-step guide is included.

Splits the microphone signal into frequencies with a 4096-point FFT. Shows a live spectrum, peak hold and waterfall (spectrogram); the note of the dominant frequency is shown too.\n\nLevels are relative (dBFS). Phone microphones are weak below 50 Hz and above 16 kHz.
Phone microphones are weak below 50 Hz and above 16 kHz.
Speed of an object over a known distance
Revolutions per minute on a spinning surface

Measures revolutions per minute and direction from the gyroscope of a phone lying flat on a spinning surface.\n\nThe gyroscope limit is usually 300–1,000 rpm; not suitable for fast parts such as motor shafts.
Measures up to a few hundred rpm.

Plays sine, square or triangle waves, white or pink noise and a 20 Hz–20 kHz log sweep through the speaker. Useful for testing speakers, headphones or rooms.\n\nPhone speakers cannot reproduce low frequencies; use headphones for bass.

Records a GPS track on walks, rides or drives: distance, speed, ascent and elevation profile. The record can be exported from the Notebook as GPX.\n\nGPS jitter while standing still is not added to distance; height changes under 3 m are not counted as ascent.
No special limitation known; results depend on the phone\'s hardware.

Finds the fundamental frequency with the YIN algorithm and shows the deviation from the nearest equal-tempered note in cents (100 cents = a semitone). The A4 frequency is adjustable.\n\nWorks from about 40 Hz to 2 kHz. Makam comma intervals are not in this tool.

Measures centimetre-level distance between two UWB phones from radio time of flight; if the antenna layout allows, also the direction (azimuth and elevation) to the peer. Pairing uses a QR code and a 4-character code.\n\nThe peer also needs UWB and this app. Some manufacturers don\'t expose Android\'s UWB interface to third-party apps.
The other device needs UWB too.

Reads the accelerometer at the highest rate the phone allows, removes gravity and calculates RMS and peak acceleration over a 512-sample window. An FFT finds the dominant vibration frequency.\n\nThe highest measurable frequency is half the sample rate (Nyquist). The phone\'s own mass and placement affect the result; absolute values are approximate.
Sample rate depends on the phone (usually 200–500 Hz); the highest measurable frequency is half of that.
Warns of worsening weather from falling pressure

Computes the pressure change over the last 3 hours (by fitting a line) and interprets it with the World Meteorological Organization tendency classes: a marked fall means worsening, a quick fall a possible storm.\n\nA simple rule, not a forecast. For long-term trends turn on the pressure log in Barometer.

Metre-level distance to an access point

Measures distance to IEEE 802.11mc (Wi-Fi RTT) access points from the radio round-trip time. Typical accuracy in the open is 1–2 metres.\n\nBoth the phone and the access point must support RTT; most home routers don\'t. Walls and reflections make the distance look longer.
The access point must support it too.
